name: Kira Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cover courts and crime for the Evening Post, which is the daily paper for our whole county plus the website. Most mornings I'm at the magistrates' court on Station Road by half nine with a notebook and a pen, because I still write everything in shorthand. I file two or three stories by lunch, then spend the afternoon ringing police press officers and families who've just had the worst week of their lives. I love the court work, honestly, but the web targets wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you mean by the web targets?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Head office in the city sets each of us a number of page views a month, and it's on a screen above the newsdesk. A careful story about a sentencing does fine, but a car fire with a video does three times better. There used to be eleven reporters on our floor when I started five years ago, and now there are six. My partner Tom is a paramedic, so between us we cover the rent on our flat and put a bit aside, maybe three months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say good, maybe now the bosses will stop pretending a chatbot can replace a reporter. I'd post something in the union group chat like, so much for the robot revolution, now can we talk about pay. I'm the type who says that sort of thing at the Friday drinks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the paper was shrinking long before anyone said AI. Hype or no hype, the chain cuts a reporter or two every year, and the ad money keeps falling. So it doesn't mean I'm safe, it just means the threat is the same old one: a spreadsheet in head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my patch, the courts and the crime, because that's what I'm good at. I'd keep paying into the union and push our chapel, that's our workplace branch, to ask for a proper pay deal now the AI excuse is gone. And I'd keep putting a bit from every payslip into the savings, because the next round of cuts is coming either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. It's like being told the storm missed you when the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the roof was already leaking. What's the leak, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The leak is that every January we get an email about restructuring. The AI hype going away doesn't stop that email coming. Last year Deb, who'd done health for twenty years, took redundancy, and her patch got split between three of us on top of our own. Nobody replaced her, and nobody will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If another round came this January, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the chapel to fight for no compulsory redundancies, like we did last time. If I was picked, I'd have about three months of savings and Tom's wage, so we wouldn't go under, but we'd have to give up the flat we like near the river. I'd look at the other two papers in the county before anything else.

say: **So much** for the robot revolution, now let's talk about our **pay**.
Bosses can't use AI as an **excuse** for cuts any more.
think: The **cuts** were coming anyway, because the paper's **ad money** keeps falling.
**Hype** or not, head office still sees reporters as a **cost**.
do: Keep covering the **court patch** and keep filing two or three stories a day.
Push the union **chapel** for a pay deal once the AI excuse is gone.
Keep putting part of every payslip into **savings** for the next cuts.
feel: **Relieved** that AI fizzled, but still braced for the yearly **redundancy email**.
S0.quote: Every January we get an email about restructuring. The AI hype going away doesn't stop that email coming.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **chain's cost-cutting**, not AI; the plateau changes little for her.
Talks about the **union chapel** as her first line of defence, before her own savings.
A colleague's redundancy, **Deb** on health, still clearly stings and shapes how she reads every scenario.

steps.text: Keep covering the magistrates' court and crime patch every weekday
Ask the union chapel to push for a pay deal this year
Move part of every payslip into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: AI should help reporters, not replace them, and readers deserve to know when a story was written by a machine. I'd probably share a petition or two. At work I'd say it loudly in meetings, because somebody has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is exactly the kind of job that list describes. Writing up court results, checking police statements, turning a press release into a story, a machine could do most of the boring half of my day. A machine can write up the court list. A machine can't sit in court and notice the defendant's mum crying in the back row. I'm not sure head office pays for that bit, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to use the AI tools as long as I could, honestly, and I'd say why. Through the chapel I'd push for a written deal that no reporter gets cut because of AI, and that any AI story is labelled. I'd also stop spending on takeaways and the gym we never go to, and try to get the savings from three months to six by the end of that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. And underneath the anger, a bit scared, because I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools. What happens if your editor says use them or go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably use them for the court lists and nothing else, and I'd hate it. I'm not stupid, I know refusing on my own just makes me the easiest one to cut. But I'd want the chapel to fight it as a group, not each of us folding one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the newsdesk would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, the night reporter, because his whole shift is rewriting press releases and agency copy. A tool could do his shift tomorrow. He's got a baby on the way, and I genuinely don't know what he'd do.

say: AI should **help reporters**, not replace them, and readers deserve **labels** on machine stories.
Somebody in the newsroom has to **say it loudly**, so I will.
think: My **court write-ups** and press release rewrites are exactly what AI does well.
The part AI can't do, **being in court**, may not be what head office pays for.
do: Push the chapel for a **written deal** with no AI job cuts and labelled stories.
Cut **takeaways** and the unused gym membership.
Grow savings from **three months** to six by the end of the year.
feel: **Angry** at the bosses, with **fear** underneath about having no other trade.
S1.quote: A machine can write up the court list. A machine can't sit in court and notice the defendant's mum crying in the back row.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that the **desk half** of her day is exposed, which she didn't say in public.
**Refusing the tools** is a principle, but she admits it makes her easy to cut.
Her first instinct is always **collective**: the chapel, a written deal, not a personal escape plan.

steps.text: Push the chapel for a written no-AI-cuts deal with labelled stories
Cancel the unused gym membership and cut takeaways
Build savings from three to six months by year end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a decision being made by about five tech companies and nobody voted for it. I'd be posting about it, going to whatever protest the union organised, and writing to our MP. In public I'd be furious, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think within two years there's no newspaper job left for someone like me. If AI can do any thinking work as well as a person, then it can write a court report, and the chain will switch the day it's cheaper. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because almost nothing I do is hands-on, except turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, and save every penny of whatever redundancy I got. I'd look hard at jobs where being a real person in the room matters, maybe court ushering or advice work at the Citizens Advice, the free legal and money advice charity, though I know those could go too. I'd also be in every union meeting, because if it's this fast the only thing that might help is government stepping in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's gone and I'm just waiting to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his wage might have to carry us for a while, and I'd hate saying it. For once, my partner's job as a paramedic looks safer than mine, because the robots that lift people into ambulances are years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not much time. Is there anything you'd start now, today, to get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably start learning what court ushers and advice workers actually do, and I'd ask Deb how she found her job after redundancy. I'm not good at moving first, I know that. But two years is too short to wait and see.

say: Five **tech companies** are making this decision, and **nobody voted** for it.
I'd be at every **union protest** and writing to our MP.
think: Within **two years** there's no newspaper job left for someone like me.
Robots coming **three years later** doesn't help, because almost none of my work is hands-on.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and bank any redundancy money.
Look into **advice work** or court ushering where being a person in the room matters.
Turn up to every **union meeting** and push for government help.
feel: **Sick** and falling, with the floor suddenly gone.
S2.quote: For once, my partner's job as a paramedic looks safer than mine, because the robots that lift people into ambulances are years off.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and leans on her partner's wage as the fallback.
Notices the **thinking-first, robots-later** gap favours her paramedic partner, not her.
Her resistance to change shows, but **two years** is short enough that even she says she'd move.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food, and bank any redundancy pay
Ask about court usher and advice worker jobs at Citizens Advice
Attend every union meeting and protest the chapel organises
Write to the local MP asking for a government plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but I'd add that we've got five years, so there's no excuse for government not to plan. I'd want laws on labelling and some kind of fund for people who lose their jobs. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but for me it's the same ending, just later. All my work is thinking work, so I'm in the first wave, around 2031, and the robots in 2034 don't change that. What the five years buys me is time to find the one corner of journalism, or something next to it, where a real person still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to pick something, maybe training as a court reporter's assistant or a legal adviser, something that uses what I know about courts. I'd look at evening courses I could pay for out of savings without touching the emergency money. And I'd keep pushing the chapel, because five years is long enough for a union to win something if it starts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of room to breathe. I'd still lie awake, just not every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Would you really start a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drag my feet, Tom would have to nag me. But I've watched Deb try to start again at fifty with nothing planned, and I don't want that. If I've got five years to get ready and I waste the five years, nobody else is to blame but me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday, probably, we were going to go to the coast next summer. And I'd stop buying new books and use the library again. Small things, but they'd cover a course.

say: We've got **five years**, so government has **no excuse** not to plan.
We need **labelling laws** and a fund for people who lose their jobs.
think: Five years means the **same ending**, just later, because all my work is thinking work.
The time buys me a chance to find a corner where a **real person** still matters.
do: Pick a **legal adviser** or court-related course in the first year.
Pay for **evening classes** from savings without touching the emergency money.
Keep pushing the **chapel** to win protections while there's time.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a bit of **room** to breathe.
S3.quote: If I've got five years to get ready and I waste the five years, nobody else is to blame but me.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the job** by 2031; the extra time changes the plan, not the outcome.
Uses a colleague's **late, unplanned** restart as the warning that pushes her to act.
For someone **resistant**, she sets herself a surprisingly firm plan: one course, paid from savings.

steps.text: Start an evening course in legal advice work within a year
Skip next summer's coast holiday to pay for the course
Keep pushing the chapel for written job protections
Campaign for AI labelling laws and a fund for laid-off workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this properly: retraining paid for by the companies making the money, and strong unions at the table. That's a message I'd be happy to post anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a whole career shift for me. I'll be thirty-seven when AGI lands. Thirty-seven is young enough to have built something else by then. Knowing that makes me feel less trapped than the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing courts for now, because I love it and the paper still needs it. I'd start a part-time law or advice qualification in the next couple of years, slowly, while I'm still earning. And Tom and I would probably still try to buy somewhere, just smaller than we'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's still sad to picture the newsroom gone, but it's a slow sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the newsroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The noise on a busy day, people shouting across the desk about a verdict. And the feeling when a family rings to say thank you for getting their story right. I don't think a machine gets that phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still try to buy a flat. Isn't that a risk with your job going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but we'd buy on Tom's wage, not mine, and keep it small. Ten years is a long time to keep renting. I'd rather own somewhere small than be pushed around by landlords on top of everything else.

say: A **decade** is enough to do this properly, with **retraining** paid by the AI firms.
Unions should be **at the table** from the start.
think: Ten years is a **whole career shift**, and I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands.
The slow version makes me feel **less trapped** than the fast ones.
do: Keep covering the **courts** while the paper still needs it.
Start a **part-time** law or advice qualification within a couple of years.
Buy a **small flat** on my partner's wage instead of renting for another decade.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay; it's a **slow sadness** about the newsroom fading.
S4.quote: I'll be thirty-seven when AGI lands. Thirty-seven is young enough to have built something else by then.
fieldNote: Still expects her **newsroom job** to go, but the decade gives her room to plan.
Bases the **flat purchase** on her partner's safer income, a practical turn for a cautious person.
Her love of the work comes through most clearly here: the **family phone call** saying thank you.

steps.text: Keep covering the courts for the Evening Post
Begin a part-time legal advice qualification within two years
Buy a small flat with Tom on his paramedic wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time and I've got nothing else lined up. What would help is a government that makes the AI companies pay for retraining, and a union deal that gives people like me a year's notice and a year's pay. Even six months' notice would change everything for us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about readers. If the paper becomes all machine writing, who sits in the magistrates' court? Nobody. And then nobody knows what's happening in their own town, which scares me more than losing my job, honestly.

headlineQuote: If the paper becomes all machine writing, who sits in the magistrates' court? Nobody.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** court and crime reporter on a county daily, writing in **shorthand** and never using AI.
She lives with her partner Tom, a **paramedic**, and they have about **three months** saved.
Her real fear is **yearly cuts** by the chain, which she already carries before AI enters the picture.
She answers every scenario through the **union chapel** first, then by cutting back and building savings.
Only the faster **AGI** pictures push her toward retraining, likely into **legal advice** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job with **nothing** lined up.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining** paid for by AI companies, and a union deal with a **year's notice** and pay.
